To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

increasing the proliferation and/or survival of new neurons within the dentate gyrum of the hippocampus, by pharmacological manipulation, results in a significant improvement in cognitive function in an animal model.
increasing the number of new granule cells in the dentate of ADX rats results in a significant improvement in cognitive performance [14,15].

(1) ADX results in the slow, progressive loss of granule neurons in the dentategyrus, (2) this results in a progressive impairment in spatial learning and memory and (3) treatment with a neurogenic drug that increases the number of newly generated neurons in the dentategyrus results in a significant attenuation of these deficits [14,15].
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether increasing the proliferation, survival and integration of new neurons may support the functional recovery of the hippocampus following damage.
the potential for the functional recovery of the dentate granule cell circuitry following a naturally occurring injury to the hippocampus.
the potential for the regeneration of hippocampus neurons to support the recovery of cognitive function after hippocampal damage.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the hippocampal granule cell population is not maintained in ADX rats.
ADX results in a slow degenerative process that causes the loss of granule cell neurons within the hippocampus.
ADX rats exhibit a selective loss of dentate granule cells that results in the onset of cognitive deficits.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
increasing adult neurogenesis can promote functional recovery of a brain circuitry damaged by slow neural degeneration.
we have shown that the loss of granule neurons is prevented in ADX rats if new neurons are added to the dentate gyrum [14].

we have shown that the selective death of granule cells in ADX rats can lead to cognitive impairment, and that increasing the proliferation and/or survival of new granule cells in the ADX model may improve cognitive function.
The main takeaway from our work is that
increasing neurogenesis in the dentate can result in functional improvement in a model of neurodegeneration.
increasing the rate of adult neurogenesis in the hippocampus may be beneficial for the treatment of memory impairments caused by hippocampal injury.
the ADX model is an effective model for studying the role of adult hippocampal neurogenesis in the functional recovery of hippocampal circuitry.
